PIPESTONE XL: A DISTRICT-SCALE NICKEL-COBALT ALLOY PROJECT
Pipestone XL is First Atlantic’s wholly owned, district-scale project spanning the entire 30-kilometre Pipestone Ophiolite Complex in central Newfoundland, a belt of ultramafic rock enriched in nickel, cobalt, and chromium. Drilling is ongoing at Alloy Max, a second large-scale zone spanning approximately 4 kilometres of strike and up to 1.5 kilometres in width, making it larger than the RPM Zone.
Awaruite at Pipestone XL is the product of serpentinization, which drove sulphur out of the system and left a sulphur-free alloy which carries no acid mine drainage risk and can be concentrated by the Company’s ONSHORE MAX™ process without smelting, roasting, or high-pressure acid leaching. AWARUITE AT PIPESTONE XL: A SMELTER-FREE NICKEL-COBALT ALLOY (Ni₃Fe)
Awaruite is a naturally occurring, magnetic, sulphur-free nickel-iron-cobalt alloy (Ni₃Fe) containing approximately 77% nickel. Because it already exists in a metallic state, awaruite can be concentrated without smelting, roasting, or high-pressure acid leaching. Mineralogical and electron microprobe analysis at the Company’s RPM Zone has confirmed the awaruite averages 77.62% nickel and 1.69% cobalt, with grades as high as 86.68% nickel and 6.05% cobalt5.
Initial metallurgical test work using the Company’s ONSHORE MAX™ (Magnetic Alloy eXtraction) process upgraded rock samples from the project’s RPM Zone into a high-grade alloy concentrate averaging 67.4% nickel and grading up to 71.9% nickel and 1.76% cobalt6. Low-intensity magnetic separation first produced a magnetic concentrate grading approximately 1.6% nickel, which flotation then upgraded to the final concentrate. By comparison, a typical nickel concentrate grades 10% to 15% nickel, according to the Nickel Institute. This concentrate can move directly to downstream battery chemical refining or the manufacture of specialty alloys and stainless steel.
The absence of sulphur reduces acid mine drainage risk and related permitting challenges, positioning Pipestone XL to supply North American industries including stainless steel, electric vehicles, aerospace, and defence.

articles.title: LNG Canada to expand operation and double international natural gas exports - The Chemical Engineer
articles.summary: LNG Canada to expand operation and double international natural gas exports  The Chemical Engineer
articles.full_text:
Led by a consortium of global energy companies, LNG Canada is set to move into its Phase 2 expansion project, which will double its liquified natural gas (LNG) export capacity from 14m t/y to 28m t/y.
LNG Canada is a joint venture including Petronas, PetroChina and Mitsubishi Corporation, and led by Shell. The project was created to develop Canada’s international LNG export industry.
The project, which is based in British Columbia, has been in development for more than a decade, with Phase 1 exporting Canada’s first-ever shipment of LNG last year to South Korea.
With its 40-year export license, LNG Canada expects the phase to produce around 28m t/y of LNG exports, generating around $50bn for the Canadian economy.
Canada has several LNG export projects based in British Columbia. The region has the second largest natural gas reserves in Canada, with the country as a whole ranking 10th in largest global reserves.
The country’s LNG exports were minimal before 2025, with virtually all exports going to the neighbouring US in 2024, according to the Canada Energy Regulator.
Now, Canada has seven projects dedicated to LNG exports, representing a capital investment of almost $109bn and a potential production capacity of 50.3m t/y.
British Columbia is strategically positioned to be within reasonable shipping distance from Asia, and LNG Canada said that its production location in Kitimat is particularly beneficial with its connection to existing infrastructure, including pipelines and and roads, and connection to local governments.
LNG Canada also operates on the traditional territory of the Haisla people, an indigenous First Nation from the Kitimat region, with a population of around 2,000 people. LNG Canada said that it is working with the Haisla Nation and the project, and has developed an equity agreement with five First Nations, representing “one of the largest Indigenous ownership positions in major Canadian infrastructure”.
The expansive Phase 2 project is expected to support 4,000 jobs during construction, with the whole project requiring “tens of thousands” of skilled workers.
Currently, the facility supports more than 400 full-time jobs, with Phase 2 expected to add 90 full-time roles, and 150 contractors.
Chris Cooper, the president and CEO of LNG Canada, said: “LNG Canada Phase 2 is another nation-building investment that demonstrates Canada can build big things when governments, First Nations partners, local communities, skilled trades, contractors and investors work together with a shared purpose.
“Phase 2 is about much more than tonnes. It will create thousands of jobs and further strengthen Canada’s role as a trusted energy partner, bringing more responsibly produced Canadian LNG to global markets while supporting long-term prosperity at home.”

articles.title: Critical minerals enter a new era of commercial supply chains - Global Mining Review
articles.summary: Critical minerals enter a new era of commercial supply chains  Global Mining Review
articles.full_text:
BGN Group and Nth Cycle highlight the push to build more integrated metals supply chains
The critical minerals industry is entering a new phase in which securing mineral resources is increasingly dependent on the ability to connect mining, processing, refining, logistics, and end markets into functioning commercial supply chains.
Across North America and Europe, a growing number of partnerships and financing arrangements are bringing different parts of the value chain closer together. Long-term offtake agreements are linking producers with customers, while new refining technologies are addressing processing bottlenecks. At the same time, companies are increasingly looking beyond individual mines towards integrated supply-chain models.
The trend is visible across commodities including nickel, cobalt, lithium, and rare earth elements (REE). While the projects vary considerably, they reflect a common industry challenge. Access to mineral resources is only one part of the equation. Turning those resources into refined materials and reliably delivering them to industrial customers requires infrastructure, technology, capital, and commercial expertise.
One example is the new partnership between BGN Group and Electro Mobility Materials Europe (EMME). In May 2026, BGN entered into a long-term metals supply agreement with the French company, under which BGN will serve as primary commercial partner. BGN will supply battery-grade nickel and cobalt while managing the global commercialisation of EMME's output.
The agreement highlights the ever-growing role of international trading and logistics companies in developing critical-minerals supply chains. Rather than simply moving commodities between markets, companies such as BGN provide the commercial links, connecting producers and processors with customers around the world.
EMME's planned project near Bordeaux represents a significant development in Europe's battery-materials sector. With an investment exceeding €500 million, the project aims to supply approximately 10% of European nickel demand and 7% of European cobalt demand for batteries by 2030.
For BGN, the agreement also marks a significant expansion of its activities in critical minerals. By combining metals supply with international sales and commercialisation capabilities, the partnership positions BGN at a crucial crossroads between production and downstream demand.
The development is part of a wider movement towards more integrated supply chains.
In the US, Nth Cycle's planned public-market transaction illustrates the growing importance of refining and processing capacity. The company announced plans in 2026 to combine with Kensington Capital V in a transaction valuing the business at approximately US$585 million. The transaction is expected to provide capital for the expansion of Nth Cycle's refining capacity.
Nth Cycle's OYSTER technology is designed to recover materials including nickel, copper, and rare earth elements from mined and recycled feedstocks. Its development reflects a broader industry effort to increase the amount of value that can be captured between raw mineral production and finished industrial materials.
Other recent transactions demonstrate different approaches to the same supply-chain challenge. Lithium Americas' Thacker Pass project has combined major project financing with downstream investment from General Motors, while Energy Fuels' agreement to acquire Australian Strategic Materials brings together rare-earth processing and alloy production capabilities across multiple jurisdictions.
Meanwhile, investments in companies such as USA Rare Earth and financing initiatives involving American Battery Technology Company demonstrate the growing range of capital structures being used to develop domestic mining and processing capacity.
Taken together, these developments suggest that the critical-minerals industry is moving towards greater vertical integration and closer commercial relationships between companies operating at different stages of the value chain.
For miners and processors, securing customers and financing is becoming as important as identifying resources. For technology companies, demonstrating that new processing methods can operate at commercial scale is increasingly critical. And for trading and logistics companies, opportunities are emerging to provide the connections that allow materials to move efficiently from producers to industrial users.
The BGN–EMME partnership illustrates this evolution clearly: as new mining and processing projects come online, the companies capable of connecting supply with international demand will become central players in the critical-minerals ecosystem.

articles.title: CBAM certificate price up nearly 10% - Balkan Green Energy News
articles.summary: CBAM certificate price up nearly 10%  Balkan Green Energy News
articles.full_text:
The price of the CBAM certificate for the third quarter of 2026 is EUR 82.32, up from around EUR 75 in the first two quarters of the year.
The price of EUR 82.32 is 9.35% higher than the second quarter’s EUR 75.28. In the first quarter, it amounted to EUR 75.36.
The European Commission noted that it would calculate each quarterly price in 2026 will be calculated during the first calendar week following the end of the relevant quarter. The calculation is based on publicly available information related to EU ETS auctions, the commission added.
Of note, the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) entered into force on January 1 this year.
Since the beginning of this year, firms in the EU that import aluminum, cement, electricity, iron and steel, hydrogen and fertilizers from non-EU countries are obliged to pay a carbon price under CBAM.
But, the deadline to submit CBAM certificates for 2026 is May 31, 2027.
All CBAM certificates will be purchased on the common central platform
According to the commission, each quarterly price in 2026 will apply to the sales of CBAM certificates corresponding to emissions in CBAM goods imported into the EU during that quarter.
Pursuant to Article 20 of Regulation (EU) 2023/956, all CBAM certificates will be purchased on the common central platform from February 2027 onwards, the commission explained.
Electricity producers and developers in the Energy Community are facing challenges
Renewable electricity producers and developers in the Energy Community are facing challenges in complying with CBAM conditions on actual emission values, which additionally increases uncertainty in projected revenues.
Power utility Elektroprivreda Crne Gore (EPCG), based in Montenegro, one of the contracting parties of the Energy Community, will pay a market price of EUR 75 for CO2 emissions, according to the company’s President of the Board of Directors Milutin Đukanović.
A few weeks ago the European Parliament backed the European Commission’s proposal to extend the carbon border tax to steel and aluminium downstream goods, including finished steel and aluminium goods, fasteners, wire, springs, and finished steel and aluminium household goods.
The United Kingdom announced that it has recognized carbon pricing schemes from the European Union and 15 countries, including Montenegro and Serbia.

articles.title: Greenland government approves Tanbreez rare earth mine plan - Mining.com
articles.summary: Greenland government approves Tanbreez rare earth mine plan  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Critical Metals (Nasdaq: CRML) has won Greenland government approval for the mining and closure plans at its Tanbreez rare earths project, clearing a major hurdle towards construction.
Tanbreez, in southern Greenland, ranks among the larger undeveloped heavy rare earth projects outside China. It has an after-tax net present value of $2.1 billion at a 15% discount rate, according to a preliminary economic assessment (PEA) issued in March 2025. The study estimated initial capital costs at $290 million.
“Approval of the mining and closure plans is a defining milestone for Tanbreez and for Critical Metals Corp.,” Chairman and CEO Tony Sage said in a release on Monday. “It gives us a clear framework through 2050 to responsibly develop one of the world’s largest heavy rare earth deposits, in partnership with the Government of Greenland and the communities of South Greenland.”
The approval comes as the U.S. and its allies step up efforts to develop critical mineral supply chains outside China. Greenland’s strategic role was highlighted again in September when the U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed a new security agreement that cited existing cooperation on minerals, economic development and investment.
Shares in Critical Metals gained 4.4% on Monday morning in New York to $7.34 apiece, valuing the company at $1.08 billion. They’ve traded in a 52-week range of $5.12 to $32.15.
Permits remain
Signed Sept. 29, the mining and closure plans set out how the mine, processing plants, port and supporting infrastructure are to be built, operated and eventually closed and rehabilitated through September 2050.
They don’t yet allow Critical Metals to begin construction of the mine. The company still requires activity-specific approvals covering environmental management, marine transport, health and safety and mineral exports, as well as a required financial security.
Construction can start once those approvals have been issued and the financial security is in place, Critical Metals said Monday.
The company’s exploitation licence, granted in 2020, requires it to provide financial security and a company guarantee by the end of this year and begin exploiting minerals by June 2029, according to its latest annual filing.
Critical Metals continues to target first ore production in the fourth quarter of 2028 or first quarter of 2029, followed by concentrate exports in the third quarter of 2029.
Project economics
The PEA outlined initial production of about 85,000 tonnes annually, with potential modular expansion to about 425,000 tonnes. Tanbreez has no mineral reserves, though an April resource put the project at nearly 45 million indicated and inferred tonnes grading 0.4% total rare earth oxides.
Critical Metals has already begun some supporting infrastructure work. In June, it said footings were underway for a pilot-plant headquarters and other project infrastructure, separate from construction of the mine itself.
The company also started a 10,000-metre drilling program in June and acquired a former cruise ship to provide accommodation for project workers.
U.S. supply
Critical Metals signed a binding 15-year offtake agreement with REalloys (Nasdaq: ALOY) in May covering 15% of Tanbreez’s initial production. REalloys plans to use the material in a U.S.-based mine-to-magnet supply chain serving defence and other industrial customers.
The project has also received a $120-million letter of interest from the U.S. Export-Import Bank for potential financing, though the funding has not yet been committed.
Critical Metals is also moving towards full ownership of Tanbreez. European Lithium (ASX: EUR), which holds the remaining 7.5% stake, is being acquired by Critical Metals in an all-stock deal announced in May. Shareholders and optionholders are due to vote Oct. 22.

articles.title: Congress Moves to Break China Rare Earth Grip Before November Deadline - Tech Times
articles.summary: Congress Moves to Break China Rare Earth Grip Before November Deadline  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
With 35 days remaining before China's expanded rare-earth export-control suspension expires, House Republicans have assembled a four-bill legislative package designed to accelerate domestic mining, create a federally backed mineral stockpile, and shield defense programs from a supply chain that Beijing has proven it can switch off. The November 10, 2026 deadline is not theoretical: yttrium oxide — used in radar systems, semiconductor coatings, and jet engine thermal barriers — has already risen approximately 140-fold in price outside China since Beijing imposed licensing controls in April 2025, a price shock that has temporarily halted production at two North American firms.
The four bills represent the most comprehensive congressional response yet to a vulnerability that has been acknowledged for years but addressed only in pieces. According to a January 2026 presidential proclamation, the United States was 100 percent import-reliant for 12 minerals deemed critical to national security and relied on imports for more than half of 29 others. For rare earth elements specifically, that dependence runs nearly 100% through Chinese processing facilities — even ore extracted from domestic mines typically travels to China for separation before returning as usable metal.
Together, the bills target three chokepoints that analysts have identified in the domestic critical minerals pipeline: slow permitting, fragile supply chains, and the absence of a strategic buffer against foreign supply disruptions.
What's in the Package
The bundle draws together legislation advancing through House committees at varying speeds since late 2025. Four bills form its core:
The Critical Mineral Dominance Act (H.R. 4090) — the furthest along of the group — passed the House 224-195, with some Democratic support, and now awaits Senate action. Sponsored by Rep. Pete Stauber (R-MN), the bill directs the Department of the Interior to address mineral supply chain vulnerabilities, including by accelerating and expanding mineral production on federal land — covering National Forest System land, public lands, and any land that may be leased for exploration, development, or production of hardrock minerals. Interior must identify priority mining projects on federal lands that can be immediately approved and take all necessary and appropriate steps to expedite those priority projects.
The Protecting Domestic Mining Act (H.R. 1501), sponsored by Rep. Jefferson Shreve (R-IN), classifies mining as covered projects under the FAST Act, ensuring that such operations are protected under the federal permitting framework. The FAST-41 process — established under the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act — sets enforceable, publicly trackable timelines for federal environmental reviews through the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council. Previously available only to transportation and energy infrastructure projects, FAST-41 was extended to critical minerals by a March 2025 executive order; this bill would lock that extension into statute.
Under FAST-41, all federal agencies with a stake in a project review coordinate on a shared public timetable posted to the Federal Permitting Dashboard, with legally trackable intermediate deadlines. The process does not bypass the National Environmental Policy Act or reduce environmental review requirements — it enforces coordination so that agencies cannot sequentially delay a project that is waiting on each other. South32's Hermosa mine in Arizona (zinc, manganese) was the first mining project to complete the FAST-41 permitting process, finishing federal permitting in 2026 after about three years — compared to an industry average of seven to ten years for traditional federal mine permitting.
The Critical Minerals Supply Chain Resiliency Act (H.R. 5929), introduced by Rep. Andy Barr (R-KY), treats actions taken by the Defense Department to support domestic critical mineral production as covered projects under the FAST Act. The bill extends FAST-41 eligibility specifically to projects funded under the executive order invoking the Defense Production Act March 2025, which authorized direct federal investment in critical mineral mining and processing. It was reported to the House with an amendment by the Committee on Natural Resources in June 2026.
The SECURE Minerals Act (H.R. 7126 / S. 3659) creates a government corporation — the Strategic Resilience Reserve Corporation of the United States — to secure US access to critical minerals through domestic and partner-country production, stable pricing, and reduced reliance on foreign supply chains. A companion Senate version, introduced in January 2026 by Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) and Todd Young (R-IN), would establish a $2.5 billion Strategic Resilience Reserve — a domestic stockpile of critical minerals designed to insulate the American economy from price manipulation and supply shocks, with governance modeled on the Federal Reserve.
The reserve's seven-member board would be authorized to sell minerals for commercial and defense use, with proceeds reinvested to sustain operations. Allied nations willing to contribute 100 million minimum in capital could participate in the stockpile structure.
"China's global dominance of critical minerals supply chains gives it significant leverage and leaves the US vulnerable to economic coercion," Sen. Young said at the bill's introduction.
The China Problem — and Its November Deadline
The urgency behind the legislative push is inseparable from China's demonstrated willingness to use mineral dominance as a foreign policy lever. China now accounts for approximately 69% of global rare-earth mine production and up to 91 percent processing capacity of refining and separation worldwide. For magnet rare earths specifically — the materials that make the permanent magnets in EV motors, wind turbines, and precision guidance systems — China controls roughly 91% of refined output and 94 percent sintered permanent magnet production.
The United States imported more than two-thirds of the rare earth elements it used in 2025, despite growing alarm in Washington over reliance on China. F-35 fighter jets and Virginia-class submarines both require rare earth materials that pass through Chinese processing.
Beijing moved to activate that leverage in April 2025, requiring companies in China to obtain government approval to export even small amounts of minerals including yttrium, dysprosium, and terbium. Shipments of those elements fell roughly 50 percent from baseline levels in the months that followed. Japan — the largest rare earth magnet producer outside China — received just 4 percent of its normal dysprosium supply after the controls took effect; Germany received none.
In October 2025, China moved to expand those controls dramatically, announcing requirements that would have extended licensing obligations to foreign-made products containing even trace quantities of Chinese-origin rare earths — a provision that could have effectively brought most of the world's electronics supply chain under Beijing's export-licensing authority. China suspended those October measures until November 10, 2026, as part of a trade truce.
But that reprieve has a hard stop — and the April 2025 controls on seven elements were never suspended at all. With the November 10 deadline now approaching, three possible policy scenarios loom: Beijing could extend the suspension, selectively reactivate controls targeting specific elements or end uses, or fully restore the October 2025 measures.
The May 2026 Trump-Xi summit produced only limited concessions — the White House said China pledged to "address US concerns" about shortages of key rare earths including yttrium, scandium, and neodymium, but China's export licensing regime remained intact and the earlier language about "effectively eliminating" export controls was dropped from the communiqué. No formal extension of the suspension was announced at any subsequent meeting, and analysis from Fitch Group's BMI concluded that China's dominance of the global rare earth supply is expected to stay firmly in place.
The International Energy Agency has warned that full implementation of China's expanded export controls — if Beijing decides to proceed — could put an estimated 6.5 trillion dollars per year of downstream production outside China at risk across the automotive, high-tech, defense, and energy sectors. The automotive sector outside China could lose more than 3 trillion, with more than 40% of those losses falling on the United States.
The Processing Bottleneck Congress Cannot Fix in 35 Days
Here is the constraint that even successful legislation cannot solve before the November deadline: the United States does not have the processing and refining infrastructure to convert domestically mined ore into the defense-grade rare earth metals and magnets its military and technology industries need.
The mine-to-magnet pipeline has four stages: mining the ore, separating it into individual rare earth oxides, converting oxides into metals and alloys, and manufacturing permanent magnets. China dominates not the first stage — rare earth ore exists in the United States, Australia, Canada, Brazil, and elsewhere — but stages two through four. China controls roughly 85-90% of global rare earth refining capacity. The United States and Europe together account for an estimated 6 to 7 percent of global rare-earth oxide separation capacity combined.
The Hermosa mine — the first to complete the FAST-41 permitting process — took approximately three years under the coordinated review. A mine starting the process today would not begin production until well into the decade. The processing and refining facilities that would receive that ore are being built, but the Pentagon's $439 million commitment to domestic rare earth supply chains and the EXIM Bank's Nebraska processing facility investment represent starting points, not solutions. articles.summary: Who Controls the Critical Minerals Powering AI?  Elements by Visual Capitalist
articles.full_text:
Three Critical Minerals Behind the AI Supply Chain
Key Takeaways:
- China accounts for 99% of estimated global processed gallium production and 69.2% of rare earth mine production.
- The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces 52% of the world’s tantalum, followed by Rwanda and Nigeria.
- These lesser-known materials are used in high-performance semiconductors, magnets, and power-management components found across AI hardware.
AI infrastructure depends on far more than chips and electricity. It also relies on a range of critical materials, including gallium, rare earths, and tantalum, that are essential to semiconductors, magnets, and power-management systems.
These three materials are highlighted in Figure 2.3 of the World Bank’s World Development Report 2026 because their production is concentrated in a relatively small number of countries.
The figures here are 2025 estimates from the U.S. Geological Survey’s Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, using processed production for gallium and mine production for rare earths and tantalum.
Gallium: China’s 99% Share
Here is the World Bank’s breakdown of estimated processed gallium production:
| Country/Economy | Share of World Production (%) | 
|---|---|
| China | 99.0 | 
| Other countries | 1.0 | 
China accounts for 99% of the total. However, that does not mean China holds 99% of the world’s gallium underground. Gallium is generally recovered as a byproduct of processing bauxite for aluminum, and China’s enormous aluminum industry has helped it develop gallium extraction at scale. Earlier oversupply and low prices also contributed to producers elsewhere exiting the market.
Gallium matters because compounds such as gallium nitride (GaN) can operate efficiently at high voltages and temperatures. These properties make gallium useful in high-performance semiconductors and power electronics, an increasingly important consideration as AI data centers require more computing power and electricity.
Rare Earths: More Than One Element
| Country/Economy | Share of World Production (%) | 
|---|---|
| China | 69.2 | 
| United States | 13.1 | 
| Australia | 7.4 | 
| Myanmar | 5.6 | 
| Thailand | 1.2 | 
| India | 0.7 | 
| Other | 2.6 | 
China produces 69.2% of the total, followed by the United States at 13.1% and Australia at 7.4%.
Despite the name, “rare earths” are actually a group of 17 elements. Different members serve different roles across computing hardware. Neodymium and praseodymium, for example, are used in powerful permanent magnets found in hard drives and other equipment, while other rare earths have applications in semiconductors, displays, optics, and data storage.
Tantalum: Power Management for AI Servers
Tantalum production has a very different geographic footprint:
| Country/Economy | Share of World Production (%) | 
|---|---|
| Congo, Dem. Rep. | 52.0 | 
| Rwanda | 16.0 | 
| Nigeria | 15.6 | 
| Brazil | 7.6 | 
| China | 3.2 | 
| Australia | 2.0 | 
| Ethiopia | 1.6 | 
| Russian Federation | 1.2 | 
| Other | 0.8 | 
The Democratic Republic of the Congo supplies 52% of estimated mine production, while Rwanda and Nigeria contribute 16% and 15.6%, respectively. Together, those three countries account for 83.6%.
Tantalum’s AI connection is largely about capacitors. Polymer tantalum capacitors can provide high capacitance in a compact package along with stable electrical performance, making them useful in demanding power systems. Industry reporting in 2026 points to AI servers as a growing source of tantalum capacitor demand.
When Mineral Supply Becomes a Strategic Bottleneck
Production concentration does not automatically translate into an AI advantage. Advanced chips, fabrication capacity, energy infrastructure, and capital all matter. However, when one or a handful of countries dominate production of a critical material, export restrictions or other supply disruptions can ripple through global technology supply chains.
That risk is already visible. China has introduced export controls on gallium-related items and selected medium and heavy rare-earth items in recent years. Those measures have encouraged governments and companies elsewhere to pursue alternative suppliers and new production capacity. In Central Africa, concentrated tantalum production presents a different set of challenges, including potential supply disruptions and responsible sourcing concerns.
As AI infrastructure expands, securing the minerals behind chips, servers, and power systems could become increasingly important alongside securing the chips themselves.

articles.title: EU Carbon Price Jumps as CBAM Certificate Hits €82.32 per Tonne - CarbonCredits.com
articles.summary: EU Carbon Price Jumps as CBAM Certificate Hits €82.32 per Tonne  CarbonCredits.com
articles.full_text:
The European Union set the Q3 2026 price for Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) certificates at €82.32 per tonne of CO₂. This provides importers with a new benchmark for the carbon cost of emissions-heavy goods entering the bloc.
The European Commission published the price on October 5, after calculating it from EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) auction prices during the third quarter. It is the highest quarterly CBAM certificate price published so far in 2026. The price rose 9.4% from €75.28/tCO₂ in Q2 and about 9.2% from €75.36/tCO₂ in Q1.
The move comes as CBAM enters its first year of full operation. Importers now bear costs tied to the carbon emissions of their products. This makes the EU’s carbon price more important for global manufacturers and exporters.
CBAM Turns Carbon Reporting Into a Financial Cost
The CBAM definitive regime took effect on January 1, 2026, replacing the transitional system that operated from 2023 through 2025. The mechanism currently covers cement, iron and steel, aluminum, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen.
Importers must report the emissions embedded in covered goods and eventually surrender the corresponding number of CBAM certificates. The system is designed to address carbon leakage.
Without CBAM, EU manufacturers covered by the EU ETS could face a carbon cost that foreign producers do not pay. This could encourage production to move outside the EU or allow more carbon-intensive imports to compete with European goods.
CBAM is intended to apply a comparable carbon cost to covered imports. The European Commission states that the mechanism aims to make sure imported products pay a carbon price similar to what EU producers pay. This also encourages cleaner production outside the EU.
An EU official recently said that starting in January 2026, CBAM will shift from reporting emissions to adding a financial cost to those emissions.
Q3 CBAM Price Climbs Nearly 10%
The new €82.32/tCO₂ price marks a clear increase during 2026. The Q3 price is important because it applies to CBAM-covered emissions from goods imported into the EU during that quarter.
However, importers do not begin buying certificates during 2026. The Commission says that approved CBAM declarants will start buying certificates in February 2027 for their imports from 2026.
The first CBAM declarations and corresponding certificate surrender are due by September 30, 2027. This gives companies time to calculate their embedded emissions, verify data, and prepare for the financial obligation.
How Much Could €82.32 Cost Importers?
The certificate price provides a straightforward way to estimate the potential carbon cost. For example, an importer with 10,000 tonnes of embedded emissions would face a gross certificate cost of approximately €823,200 at the Q3 2026 price.
At 100,000 tonnes, the figure rises to about €8.23 million.
The actual liability can be lower because CBAM allows importers to deduct a carbon price already paid in the country where the goods were produced. The final number of certificates also depends on the rules for calculating embedded emissions and the applicable free-allocation adjustment. That makes emissions data increasingly valuable.
The Commission has released guidance for specific sectors, including cement, hydrogen, fertilizers, iron and steel, aluminum, and electricity. It aims to help companies calculate embedded emissions during the set period.
For exporters, cleaner production can therefore become a competitive advantage. Lower embedded emissions mean fewer CBAM certificates are ultimately required.
Weekly CBAM Pricing Starts in 2027
The €82.32 price is also important because it represents the last phase of the EU’s temporary quarterly pricing system. For 2026, the Commission calculates four prices, one for each calendar quarter.
From 2027 onward, certificate prices will be calculated and published weekly. The methodology is designed to track the EU ETS more closely by using the relevant auction prices for EU ETS allowances. This means importers will face a more dynamic carbon price environment.
The EU’s approach aims to keep the carbon cost for imports aligned with the carbon cost faced by European producers under the ETS. It also means companies will need to pay closer attention to carbon price movements when planning procurement, production and investment.
For businesses importing large quantities of emissions-intensive materials, carbon pricing could increasingly become part of ordinary supply chain cost management.
EU Could Expand CBAM’s Reach
CBAM is not necessarily staying limited to its current product categories. In June, the European Commission welcomed a Council agreement to extend CBAM to specific downstream goods and strengthen anti-circumvention measures.
The proposal aims to stop companies from sidestepping the rules. They can’t process covered materials into specific products outside the EU and then import them. This could expand the number of businesses exposed to the mechanism.
At the same time, the EU recently assessed its 50-tonne de minimis threshold. From April 2025 to March 2026, the Commission found that the threshold would exempt only 0.87% of embedded emissions. This is below the 1% limit set by the regulation.
The threshold was introduced to reduce the administrative burden on smaller importers. The Commission previously estimated that it would exempt about 182,000 importers while still covering more than 99% of emissions within CBAM’s scope.
The result is a system designed to reduce paperwork for small shipments without removing most emissions from the mechanism.
Carbon Pricing Is Expanding Beyond Europe
The CBAM price arrives as carbon pricing continues to expand globally. The World Bank’s State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026 report found that 87 carbon pricing policies were operating worldwide as of 2026.
Direct carbon pricing now covers over 29% of global greenhouse gas emissions. In 2025, carbon pricing systems generated over $107 billion in government revenue. The average direct carbon price reached nearly $21/tCO₂e.
- The EU’s €82.32 CBAM certificate price is therefore substantially above the global average direct carbon price.
However, the comparison is not like-for-like. The World Bank figure includes various carbon taxes and emissions trading systems. In contrast, CBAM is tied to the EU’s carbon market and targets embedded emissions in certain imports.
Still, the trend is clear: Carbon is increasingly becoming a direct economic cost in international trade.
EU Climate Policy Is Tightening the Long-Term Signal
CBAM is part of the EU’s broader climate strategy.
The bloc set a target in 2026 to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by 90% from 1990 levels by 2040. At least 85% of this reduction must happen within the EU, and up to 5% can come from international carbon credits. The bloc remains committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050.
CBAM supports that trajectory by extending the carbon price signal beyond EU borders for covered products. The policy also interacts directly with the EU ETS, where European industrial producers already face carbon costs.
As the EU ETS gradually cuts free allocation for sectors under CBAM, the border mechanism will become more important. This gives manufacturers a stronger incentive to reduce emissions rather than simply absorb higher carbon costs.
The shift also creates stronger incentives for exporters to provide accurate, verified emissions data. Companies with lower actual emissions can potentially reduce their CBAM liability compared with producers relying on higher default values.
From 2027, the move to weekly certificate pricing will make the system even more closely tied to carbon market movements.
CBAM Is Becoming a Global Trade Signal
The European Commission’s €82.32/tCO₂ Q3 price marks another step in the transition from carbon reporting to carbon pricing at the border. The price is almost 10% above the Q2 benchmark.
The EU is also getting ready for weekly pricing starting in 2027, with the first certificate surrender deadline set for September 2027. At the same time, carbon pricing is spreading globally. The World Bank reports that direct carbon pricing now covers nearly 30% of global emissions.
For companies exporting emissions-intensive products to Europe, the implications are clear. Carbon emissions are no longer only an environmental metric. Under CBAM, they can directly affect the cost of accessing the EU market.
As the mechanism expands and the EU continues tightening its climate targets, the ability to measure, verify, and reduce embedded emissions is likely to become an increasingly important part of international industrial competitiveness.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Rare Earths and the Geopolitics of the Stilwell Road - Geopolitical Monitor
articles.summary: Myanmar’s Rare Earths and the Geopolitics of the Stilwell Road  Geopolitical Monitor
articles.full_text:
Myanmar’s rare earth sector is attracting new attention as India, the United States, and other countries look for ways to diversify critical mineral supplies. Myanmar has something these countries need: rare earth resources, including heavy rare earth elements (HREE) such as dysprosium (Dy) and terbium (Tb). But there is a problem. Many of these resources are located in northern Myanmar, where armed conflict, contested authority, and weak infrastructure make them difficult to turn into a reliable alternative source of supply.
HREE extraction is concentrated in Kachin State, where the armed Kachin Independence Army (KIA)/Kachin Independence Organisation (KIO) has significant influence and control. The area is close to the historic Stilwell Road, also known as the Ledo Road, a Second World War supply route, connecting Ledo in India’s Assam region with Kunming in China through northern Myanmar. The road has attracted renewed interest not because of military logistics, but for a very different strategic resource: rare earth elements.
What Makes Kachin’s Rare Earths Valuable
Dysprosium and terbium are highly sought because they enhance the thermal performance of permanent magnets used in applications such as electric motors, advanced electronics, and defence technologies. Myanmar’s Kachin deposits therefore matter not simply because the country produces rare earths, but because some of its deposits contain elements that are difficult to replace. The country is already a significant producer, with the US Geological Survey (USGS) estimating that Myanmar produced approximately 22,000 tonnes of rare earth oxide (REO) equivalent in 2025, after accounting for 7.1% of global production in 2024. But production is only one part of the story. Myanmar’s major weakness is that it can extract rare earths but lacks the refining and manufacturing capacity needed to process them into higher-value industrial products. Therefore, much of the strategic industrial value is created outside the country.
China remains central to this equation as it has the processing capacity at a scale that Myanmar has not. Myanmar’s dependence on China is also visible in the trade data. S&P Global estimates that Myanmar supplied about 52.8% of China’s rare earth imports in 2025. This means that Myanmar has become an important upstream supplier of heavy rare earth feedstock to China’s rare earth processing ecosystem. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that China accounted for about 91% of global refining output of magnet rare earths and 94% of sintered permanent magnet manufacturing in 2024.
India and the US Look for Another Route
India is trying to change its own position in this market. New Delhi has identified critical minerals as important to manufacturing, energy, telecommunications, and defence, while also seeking to expand domestic rare earth processing and permanent magnet production. In November 2025, the Indian government approved a Rs. 7,280 crore (approximately US$760 million) scheme to establish 6,000 metric tonnes per annum (MTPA) of sintered rare earth permanent magnet (REPM) manufacturing capacity. But building factories does not solve the problem of where the raw materials will come from. India still needs reliable sources outside its own borders. Myanmar borders India and possesses the rare earths India needs, making it difficult for New Delhi to ignore.
The United States has a broader interest in the same effort. Washington has identified the need to diversify critical mineral sources, strengthen supply chain resilience, and reduce dependence on foreign processing and supply networks. The January 2026 presidential proclamation on processed critical minerals specifically warned that the US remains heavily dependent on foreign sources and lacks sufficient domestic processing capacity. It also called for greater diversification of supply and stronger domestic capabilities. In addition, the US interest in Myanmar’s rare earths is not entirely theoretical. Competing proposals were put forward to the Trump administration to gain access to Myanmar’s heavy rare earths and reduce dependence on China. The ideas ranged from engagement with Myanmar’s military authorities to possible negotiations involving the armed KIA, direct engagement with the KIA, and cooperation with India to process Myanmar heavy rare earths.
For India and the US, this creates a common interest in finding alternative sources and supply routes. The two countries signed the Strategic Critical Minerals Cooperation Framework in May 2026, reflecting this wider objective. Myanmar is relevant to that effort because of both its resources and its location. Kachin State borders China, while India’s northeast lies to the west across Myanmar. This makes northern Myanmar a potential link between two markets looking for alternatives to China-dominated supply chains. But access to the resources is only part of the problem. The minerals still have to move from the mining areas to processing and manufacturing facilities. That brings the question of routes back into the picture—and with it, the Stilwell Road.
Reviving the Stilwell Road
The road has the potential to establish an alternative transport corridor for rare earths between northern Myanmar and northeast India, with onward access to processing facilities in mainland India. However, it passes through one of Asia’s most contested borderlands, where international borders overlap with ethnic territories, armed organizations, and competing claims of authority. Kachin State illustrates the problem. The Myanmar government does not exercise uncontested control across all the areas where the resources are found or along every route they would need to travel. This creates a practical dilemma for India. Any effort to develop a route through northern Myanmar would require dealing with the authorities that control the territory, local communities, security conditions, and Myanmar’s central authorities. At the same time, bypassing the Myanmar authorities and engaging directly with the KIA/KIO would carry its own political and diplomatic implications for New Delhi.
The route also passes through Pangsau Pass, in the Naga borderlands that extend across the India-Myanmar frontier. Naga political movements have consistently contested the authority of both India and Myanmar in Naga areas, adding another layer of complexity. This makes the Stilwell Road more than a road connecting two countries. Any attempt to develop it as part of a wider economic or mineral corridor would have to operate in a borderland where national borders, local communities, armed groups, and competing political claims all meet.
The Mine-to-Factory Problem
The challenge is not simply reaching Myanmar’s rare earth deposits. The proposals put forward to the Trump administration to gain access to Myanmar’s rare earths and reduce their flow to China show that mineral access is also tied to the political and security conditions around the mines and the routes leading out of them. The harder task is moving the minerals from the mine to the factory. China already has much of that system in place. Myanmar’s rare earths are already feeding Chinese supply chains, linking mining areas in Kachin State with processing and manufacturing facilities farther north in China. For China, the issue is largely how to maintain an established supply line. India faces a different situation. Although it shares a border with Myanmar and is close to its rare earth deposits, the areas where many of the resources are found are not under the uncontested control of Myanmar’s central government, and parts of the routes leading out of Kachin are influenced by armed groups, competing claims, and other local authorities.
For India, the question of how those minerals could move out of northern Myanmar brings the Stilwell Road, an old wartime supply route, back into focus. The road is not yet a rare earth corridor, and there is no guarantee that it will become one. Its location puts it close to Myanmar’s rare earth deposits and within a borderland where Chinese economic networks, Indian connectivity interests, and wider US efforts to diversify critical-mineral supplies meet. The question is whether the road can become part of a supply chain that currently runs largely through China, given the political and security conditions surrounding it.

articles.summary: OPEC+ is keeping oil output targets frozen for November as Iran war disrupts Gulf exports  Quartz
articles.full_text:
Seven core OPEC+ members agreed Sunday to hold November production targets at the same levels required in September, leaving output policy unchanged as the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran continues to suppress Gulf exports.
The seven countries — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman — made the decision in a brief online meeting. The group said its members reiterated their commitment to comply with the Declaration of Cooperation, and announced the next meeting for November 1.
Export disruptions from the war have held Gulf OPEC+ producers far short of their output ceilings, with shipment volumes running at 60% to 80% of normal levels over recent months, according to Reuters. OPEC data shows the seven core members' August output reached 25 million barrels per day, a gain of 630,000 barrels per day over July, though that figure remains about 5 million barrels per day short of where production stood before the war in February.
Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from around $73 before the conflict began in late February. Oil prices fell on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves, according to Reuters.
UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said in a note cited by Reuters that despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, output among the seven members remains well below quota. "Consequently, the oil market remains tight," Staunovo said.
Throughout 2026, OPEC+ has continued to lift its output targets in the wake of a prolonged cutting cycle, yet the conflict has largely prevented those paper increases from materializing as actual barrels, according to Reuters. Broader production curbs totaling roughly 2 million barrels per day remain active across most of the group's members.
Any meaningful changes to output policy are unlikely before 2027. The conflict has also delayed a key capacity review that OPEC+ commissioned in late 2025 to set individual members' 2027 production quotas. The review, originally due by the end of September, is not expected to wrap up before mid-November, as the conflict has made it difficult to reliably project how much production capacity member countries will be able to sustain going forward.
U.S. petroleum consultant DeGolyer and MacNaughton is conducting capacity estimates for members excluding Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, which are under U.S. sanctions. Nations that receive lower capacity assessments risk being assigned smaller production quotas, while members that have expanded infrastructure may use the results to argue for larger allowances. The capacity review has long been a politically sensitive issue within the group.

articles.title: LNG Export Capacity Is Set to Grow 50% by 2030. Here's What It Means for U.S. Energy Stocks. - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: LNG Export Capacity Is Set to Grow 50% by 2030. Here's What It Means for U.S. Energy Stocks.  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
Supply shocks from Russia's war in Ukraine and the Iran war have led to the prices of liquified natural gas (LNG) doubling since the start of the year. Those shocks are just minor tremors compared to the earthquake underway that will affect any energy stock that touches LNG.
Between 2025 and 2030, facilities capable of exporting more than 330 billion cubic meters per year (bcm/yr) of LNG are scheduled to open, doubling the current LNG export capacity, according to data from the International Energy Agency.
These facilities belong to projects that were already under construction and had received their final investment decision (FID), the official agreement to finance and build them, as of 2025. This expansion represents the largest increase in export capacity in history. Ultimately, the way this influx of natural gas unfolds will heavily influence global gas supplies and prices.
That's a huge increase, but even that rate of expansion may not be enough to keep up with demand. The growth of LNG export capacity and the rise in LNG demand will have a big ripple effect on energy stocks. Let's see how.
Initially, the new LNG projects may hold prices down
Shell (SHEL +1.14%) projects global LNG demand to rise by around 65% by 2050, to nearly 700 million tonnes a year. ExxonMobil (XOM +0.29%), meanwhile, pointing to increased demand in Asia, forecasts that its annual LNG sales will reach 50 million tons by 2030 and continue to rise beyond the current decade.
However, in the short term, particularly when the Iran war ebbs, there's a good chance that initially supply will outpace growth in global demand, and benchmark natural gas prices, such as Europe's TTF and Asia's JKM, are expected to face strong downward pressure.
Companies heavily focused on gas extraction without locked-in long-term contracts will see squeezed profit margins as market prices drop from recent historical highs. Facilities relying on spot market sales, selling gas day-to-day, will face severe revenue pressure.
Key Data Points
Energy integrated energy majors such as Shell, ExxonMobil, Chevron (CVX +0.54%) and TotalEnergies (TTE -0.46%), will be insulated from some of the changes because they have long-term take-or-pay contracts. However, over time, their expiring contracts will likely be renegotiated at much shorter durations and at lower prices. That should put pressure on the margins of these energy majors.
The majors that adapt quickly to move cargoes to areas where demand and prices remain highest will thrive, but major oil and gas companies will face challenges.
Midstream operators should thrive
Midstream operators -- the companies responsible for gathering, processing, transporting, and storing natural gas -- are among the biggest long-term winners of the expanded LNG export capacity.
While upstream producers deal with volatile commodity prices, midstream companies typically operate on toll-road-like commercial models. Moving 330+ bcm/yr of additional gas requires massive throughput, creating a major growth runway for midstream infrastructure.
They get paid based on the volume of natural gas they move in their pipelines, not on the spot price. Pipeline operators feeding Gulf Coast terminals will see near 100% capacity utilization on their transmission systems.
The larger midstream operators with major pipelines that connect to the Gulf of Mexico stand to benefit in the long term, including Kinder Morgan (KMI +2.39%), Williams Companies (WMB +2.23%), Enterprise Products Partners (EPD +1.25%), and Enbridge (ENB +1.09%).
However, to keep up, these companies will incur significant capital expenditures as large-diameter, high-pressure natural gas pipelines are being constructed to directly link gas fields to coastal export plants.
Key Data Points
Energy infrastructure and logistics companies should benefit
Any rise in LNG exports means that shipping, storage, and regasification infrastructure companies win regardless of where commodity prices end up. Stocks that could easily grow include LNG carrier operators such as Flex LNG (FLNG -0.89%) and Golar LNG (GLNG +0.58%). They should also see elevated charter demand to move the increased cargo volume across oceans.
Other companies that provide floating storage and regasification units, such as Excelerate Energy (EE +1.38%) and Höegh LNG (HMLPF +1.97%), will likely build receiving ports in emerging markets to catch cheap gas.
The trend will shake up the industry
The additional LNG export projects represent the largest and fastest wave of supply build-out in the history of the gas industry, driven primarily by mega-projects taking shape in the United States, Qatar, and Russia.
There will be winners and losers from this sea change. It's hard to say which major oil and gas producers will adapt and which ones will struggle. However, there are plenty of likely winners in LNG logistics, including midstream operators, LNG tankers, and storage companies, as they stand to benefit the most in the long term from the massive surge in gas throughput and transport demand.

The global nickel market is expected to remain in surplus next year as Indonesian output recovers on potentially higher mining quotas and lower sulphur and sulphuric acid prices, Japan’s top nickel smelter Sumitomo Metal Mining (TYO: 5713) said on Tuesday.
SMM forecasts a global nickel surplus of 34,000 metric tons in 2027, narrowing from 38,000 tons this year. Indonesian production of low-grade nickel pig iron (NPI) is expected to rebound 11.9% to 1.88 million tons, according to the company’s half-year market outlook.
Indonesian NPI production is seen falling 2.3% in 2026 after rising 12.4% in 2025 due to government cuts in mining quotas. Indonesia accounts for more than 60% of global nickel output.
Potentially higher mining quotas could boost NPI output, while lower sulphur and sulphuric acid prices, key inputs in nickel production, could increase production of nickel intermediates such as mixed hydroxide precipitate, SMM General Manager Shirou Imai told reporters.
Global nickel demand is forecast to rise 6% to 3.92 million tons in 2027, supported by steady stainless steel consumption and rising demand for speciality steel used in AI data centres. Supply is seen rising 5.8% to 3.96 million tons.
“In 2027, we anticipate that a recovery in NPI production will ease the shortage of Class 2 nickel, while the continued decline in Chinese cathode production will soften the surplus of Class 1 nickel,” Imai said, adding that the overall market would remain in surplus.
Class 1 nickel is high-purity refined metal used in batteries and other applications, while Class 2 mainly comprises NPI and ferronickel used in stainless steel.
SMM, which supplies cathode materials for Panasonic (TYO: 6752) lithium-ion batteries used in Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) EVs, expects global nickel demand for batteries to rise to 620,000 tons next year from 560,000 tons in 2026, driven by continued growth in Chinese EV sales.

Japan's Iwatani Corporation and Cosmo Energy Holdings announced on Tuesday that they have reached a final investment decision to jointly develop a hydrogen supply chain at Cosmo's Chiba refinery near Tokyo, according to MiningWeekly.com. Operations at the site are scheduled to begin in 2030.
Under the plan, Cosmo Oil, a unit of Cosmo Energy, will bring an idled hydrogen production plant at the refinery back into service with a capacity of roughly 80 tons per day, backed by an investment of about 20-billion yen, equivalent to approximately $126.5-million.
Iwatani Industrial Gases, a unit of Iwatani, will construct a liquefied hydrogen plant with a capacity of 11.6 tons per day, at an investment of about 30-billion yen.
Cosmo intends to use the hydrogen in its refining operations and will supply part of the output to Iwatani, which will liquefy the hydrogen and distribute it to domestic customers.
The companies expect the project to secure a stable hydrogen supply for the refinery while expanding Iwatani's domestic liquefied hydrogen production capacity. Iwatani supplies about 70% of Japan's hydrogen.
According to the two companies, consolidating hydrogen production will lower costs relative to separate investments and support the development of a competitive domestic hydrogen supply chain.
Engineering, procurement and construction work will be led by Cosmo Iwatani Hydrogen Engineering, a joint venture the companies established in 2023.
The project converts the companies' capital and business alliance, agreed in April 2024, into a concrete investment. It follows Iwatani's acquisition of an additional stake in Cosmo in 2023, which made Iwatani the largest shareholder.

articles.title: S’pore mulls energy cluster on Tekong; including third LNG terminal and electricity import facilities - The Straits Times
articles.summary: S’pore mulls energy cluster on Tekong; including third LNG terminal and electricity import facilities  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE – The military island of Pulau Tekong could potentially host Singapore’s third liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal, hydrogen-compatible natural gas power plants and facilities for importing electricity.
The Energy Market Authority (EMA) on Oct 6 said it is studying the feasibility of building a 200ha energy infrastructure cluster on the island located off Singapore’s north-eastern coast, to strengthen the nation’s energy security and support its transition to greener energy sources.
This is equivalent to the size of 288 football fields.
EMA said: “Electricity demand in Singapore will grow as our economy continues to expand. While EMA studies the viability of diverse energy pathways, there is a need to plan ahead for new energy infrastructure to meet our long-term power demand.”
Singapore currently relies on imported natural gas, a fossil fuel, for about 93% of its energy needs.
It is currently building its second LNG terminal at Jurong Port. The terminal will be operational by the end of the decade. The Republic’s first LNG terminal began operations on Jurong Island in 2013.
But the country is also looking at alternative energy sources, including the use of hydrogen as a cleaner fuel, and importing electricity directly from its neighbours, to increase its energy security in a climate-friendly way.
To assess the feasibility of building an energy cluster on Pulau Tekong, EMA will appoint a consultant by mid-2027 to develop a proposed masterplan for the cluster. This study is expected to take two years to complete.
The Straits Times’ checks on tender documents published on Oct 5 on government procurement portal GeBiz showed that the study will assess the feasibility of accommodating approximately 6 gigawatts of domestic power generation and 2 gigawatts of electricity imports via three designated sea corridors.
For context, Singapore had the capacity to produce about 13 gigawatts of electricity in the first half of 2025. To date, Singapore has 13 electricity import projects in the works, with a combined capacity of more than 9 gigawatts. The projects cover solar, wind and hydropower from Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Vietnam and Australia.
The study will also look into accommodating nine to 15 telecommunication submarine cables via three to five designated sea corridors connecting to the area within Pulau Tekong.
EMA will share three development scenarios with the awarded consultant. Each scenario will outline key areas such as the type of energy mix, their capacity and proposed development timelines. The tender also mentions biomass and geothermal power plants.
The three scenarios will be shared only with the awarded consultant.
The consultant has to develop a masterplan for each scenario that identifies the optimal approach to use the 200ha of land for facilities including power plants, an LNG terminal, gas facilities, electricity import facilities, substations and a cable tunnel building, stated tender documents.
The feasibility study should also assess the technical, regulatory, environmental and aviation considerations linked to the proposed energy cluster.
During the National Day Rally in August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that 500ha of land, about the size of Toa Payoh, could be set aside for civilian use on Pulau Tekong, with more reclamation works at the southern end of the island in the pipeline.
He also said studies are under way to see if it is feasible to build undersea tunnels linking the mainland to Pulau Tekong, to make it easier for people to reach the island.
EMA’s chief executive Puah Kok Keong said: “Energy is a critical resource to support Singapore’s continued development and growth. It is vital that we plan ahead for our future energy infrastructure needs.”
If the island’s energy cluster plan materialises, the cluster will play an important role to meet Singapore’s growing energy needs, he added.
Pulau Tekong could even be a second major energy cluster for Singapore, after Jurong Island, said Tan-Soo Jie Sheng, director of the Institute for Environment and Sustainability at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.
It can be a multi-fuel energy hub, where some energy sources may have lower use because they serve as a back-up, instead of running all the time.
“But we gain energy resilience in return as we become less dependent on any single fuel, technology, supplier or geographical location,” Tan-Soo said.
Tekong’s location could also be advantageous for electricity imports from Riau Islands in Indonesia, he added.
While a potential third LNG terminal shows that natural gas is expected to remain an important part of Singapore’s energy mix for some time, more LNG import does not necessarily mean more gas consumption, Tan-Soo said.
Higher capacity for natural gas could provide energy security and flexibility, especially in crises, before greener alternatives are available at scale.
“LNG terminals and gas-fired power plants are long-lived investments, so ideally their economics should not depend on Singapore maintaining high levels of gas consumption for decades,” Tan-Soo added.

FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt
A 700MW cross-border transmission line will bring affordable power to the DRC's Copperbelt, unlock new mining and industrial capacity, open export routes for licensed Zambian power producers, and enable new generation.
FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt.
FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt
A 700MW cross-border transmission line will bring affordable power to the DRC's Copperbelt, unlock new mining and industrial capacity, open export routes for licensed Zambian power producers, and enable new generation
Published on
6 Oct 2026
Kinshasa, 6 October 2026 – The Strategic Investment Fund of the Democratic Republic of the Congo ("FIS-RDC"), Enterprise Power DRC SARL ("EnPower"), Trafigura and Gridworks Development Partners (together, "the Parties") have signed a Strategic Framework Agreement to jointly finance, build and operate a 200km high-voltage power line connecting Kalumbila, Zambia, with Kolwezi, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The Kalumbila–Kolwezi Interconnector Project ("KKIP") will strengthen the DRC's connection to the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), the regional body that links national grids and allows countries to trade power across borders. The project has reached the final stage of development, with all necessary concessions, licences and authorisations secured. It has an estimated construction cost of USD300 million.
KKIP will deliver benefits on both sides of the border: a new source of reliable, affordable power for the DRC's mining and industrial sectors, and new export capacity and transmission opportunities for Zambian power producers. The line will have a thermal capacity of 700MW, enabling up to 550MW of competitively priced electricity to be imported into the Copperbelt mining region of the DRC. The line design allows for a future capacity increase to over 1GW.
The Parties and financing
FIS-RDC, EnPower and Gridworks have confirmed their intention to invest equity in KKIP, with Gridworks as lead equity investor and majority shareholder. The Parties are in discussions with Zambian entities about taking a stake in the project. EnPower is the project developer, a licensed Congolese power trader and a SAPP member. Gridworks is a specialist transmission and distribution developer owned and funded by British International Investment, the UK Government’s development finance institution. Trafigura, a market leader in the global commodities industry, has agreed to arrange a significant share of the project's debt financing.
For FIS-RDC, the transaction supports the DRC Government's objective of investing in strategic infrastructure with wider economic benefits. It is the first investment announced by FIS-RDC since its creation in October 2025.
Benefits for the DRC
KKIP will help address the country's structural energy deficit of more than 1GW. It is expected to:
Supply electricity from across Southern Africa to power Congolese mining and industry, supporting social and economic development in local communities.
Enable the development of mining and refining projects currently on hold due to a lack of available, cost-effective baseload power.
Increase mining and refining output, generating greater fiscal contributions for the DRC.
Deliver broader benefits for the DRC by expanding access to reliable, affordable power for communities and businesses, supporting local enterprise and jobs, and contributing to economic diversification.
Benefits for Zambia
KKIP will create export opportunities for Zambian power producers, provide transmission capacity for licensed operators, and help spur the development of new generation. The participation of FIS-RDC, alongside Gridworks and Trafigura, will also strengthen cooperation between the DRC and Zambian governments and create a platform for long-term investment. Discussions are already underway with Zambian entities on potential co-investment.
Emile Osumba, CEO of FIS-RDC, said: "KKIP is the Fund's inaugural transaction, and it reflects precisely the mandate entrusted to us by the Government. By helping close the Copperbelt's power deficit, the project will unlock industrial growth, skilled jobs and fiscal revenue for the DRC. By backing a project led by a private Congolese developer, FIS-RDC is demonstrating that sovereign capital can act as a catalyst for private investment rather than a substitute for it. And by co-investing alongside credible and experienced partners such as Gridworks, we are building the track record that will allow the Fund to mobilise further capital for the country's strategic infrastructure."
Marc Orphanides, Managing Director of EnPower, added: “This agreement is an important milestone towards executing this strategic transmission infrastructure, which will add significant capacity to meet the ever-growing power demand of the DRC mining industry. We are grateful to the authorities, stakeholders and communities in the DRC and Zambia, as well as the International Finance Corporation, for their support to KKIP, which will be the first privately developed and financed cross-border transmission infrastructure on the African continent.”
Gonzalo De Olazaval, Global Head of Metals and Minerals at Trafigura, commented: “Trafigura is proud to support this landmark power project in the DRC, part of our broader power strategy in Africa. Reliable, competitively priced power is a critical enabler of economic growth across the continent, and Trafigura is well placed to bring together the investment, infrastructure and partnerships needed to make these projects a reality. KKIP has the potential to unlock industrial growth in the DRC and Zambia, while also supporting job creation and local communities in both countries.”
Chris Flavin, CEO of Gridworks, said: “Gridworks is proud to be the lead equity investor in KKIP. This is an important regional integration project. Zambia and the DRC both stand to benefit from closer interconnection, and this project will give the Copperbelt access to reliable, competitively priced power and lay the foundation for further cross-border transmission investment across Southern Africa. While the project is anchored by mining offtake, there is capacity on the line to serve the wider population too. Connecting regional power markets and supporting efficient energy trading is key to sustained economic growth in the region. We look forward to working alongside our partners to deliver this important infrastructure."

articles.full_text:
Oil prices rose more than 1% on Wednesday, with Brent crude crossing the $101-a-barrel mark as fresh supply risks outweighed rising optimism due to increased Middle East crude supplies.
WTI crude rose 1.05% to $90.38 a barrel, while Brent crude gained 1.02% to $101.60 as supply concerns emerged in Saudi Arabia and the US oil and refining sector.
The latest concerns came from both sides of the global oil supply chain. According to US forecasters, a storm developing in the Gulf of Mexico is expected to become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days and is likely to affect oil and gas facilities.
The areas in the storm's path account for 15% of US crude production and 5% of the country's natural gas production. Six refineries could also be affected. Refineries located in US Gulf states represent about 50% of the country's total refining capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day (bpd).
The prospect of disruption has emerged even as oil supplies from the Middle East have increased. Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman on Tuesday said that supply had been rising, with the East-West pipeline reaching 5.8 million barrels a day.
The head of Vitol said that around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products had been shipped out of the Middle East by tankers over the previous seven to 10 days.
US inventory data, however, offered a mixed picture. According to market sources citing by Reuters, crude and gasoline inventories declined last week, while distillate stocks increased marginally. US crude inventories fell by 2.09 million barrels in the week ended October 2.
Meanwhile, tensions around Saudi Arabia have added another risk to regional supply. The Saudi aviation authority said airports in Jazan and Najran were attacked twice on Monday evening as hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis escalated.
The attacks came as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pursued a major offensive to regain territory from the Houthis after weeks of rebel advances. Saudi Arabia has increased airstrikes in support of the campaign.
Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at X Analysts in Sydney, said the attacks and refinery outages could continue to support higher oil prices.
“Attacks and refinery outages are likely to keep the cracks elevated and scarcity will transmit to crude. Prices will stay elevated near a $100 level without any material de-escalation emerging,” Sahdev said.
The wider tensions involving Iran have also remained unresolved. US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that there was uncertainty over who was running Iran during the eight-month US-Israeli war with Iran.
"Their leaders are gone, their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country," Trump said.
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said on Sunday that Washington knows very well who its counterpart is in Iran and how the decision-making system in the country works.
